entries.title: White Sox Pope Leo night draws out thousands for pope hats and Catholic fanfare
entries.summary: <p>Cynthia Castañeda has been Catholic as long as she’s been a White Sox fan — for her entire life.</p><p>Despite clear weather after severe storms that could only be described as an act of God, she and her husband Michael made the trip from Indiana to make the game and, more importantly, to celebrate Pope Leo XIV.</p><p>They were among the tens of thousands lining up outside Guaranteed Rate Field who collected a complementary Sox-themed pope hat.</p><p>The couple, who both grew up on the South Side, are hoping the Sox-loving pope's presence could bring about a new championship era.</p><p>“It makes for a deeper connection knowing he’s a Sox fan,” she said. “I hope he’s back for another World Series win.”</p><p>The giveaway was initially intended for just 2,500 fans with special tickets. But the giveaway soon expanded to the entire stadium of nearly 41,000.</p><p>As for making the pope-themed game an annual tradition? </p><p>“We’ll see,” says Brooks Boyer, White Sox executive vice president. “We wanna be super respectful to the pope, to the Vatican. Hopefully this represents a tie to his childhood team, doing it the exact right way.”</p><p>Vendors outside the stadium sold pope pins, hats and shirts bearing the classic Sox batter logo adorning the papal crown.</p><p>The hats weren’t the game's only religious fare.</p><p>Famed former White Sox organist Nancy Faust returned to her seat to perform the National Anthem after the first pitch was thrown out by Sister Mary Jo Sobieck of the Dominican Sisters of Springfield. </p><p>It was Sobieck’s second time at the mound. In 2018, she <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-saturday/2019/7/6/20684123/espy-2019-award-nominee-sister-mary-jo-white-sox-strike" target="_blank" ><u>grabbed headlines tossing heat</u></a> across the plate for another ceremonial first pitch.</p><p>The pregame ceremony included the handover of an oversize check totaling $14,000 to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2024/06/04/augustinian-catholic-order-clergy-sex-abuse-richard-mcgrath" target="_blank" ><u>Midwest Augustinian Province</u></a>, the order to which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/05/09/pope-leo-cardinal-robert-prevost-midwest-augustinians-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>then-Fr. Robert Prevost once belonged</u></a>. Students from Our Lady of Mount Carmel Academy’s kids’ conclave joined players on the field briefly.</p><p>Preceding the seventh inning stretch, the team held a fifth inning “Peace be with you,” led by Evergreen Park and Marist High School alum Father Tom Hurley and comedian Pat McGann.</p><p>Not everyone was there for His Holiness.</p><p>Michael Rodriguez, a lifelong Sox fan, arrived with loved ones to celebrate his 29th birthday.</p><p>Rodriguez called it “God’s will” that the game landed the day before his birthday and brought him back to the stadium for the first time in five years.</p><p>“Growing up I was able to see the fireworks from my house in Pilsen, and it was always a great feeling,” Rodriguez said. “It still makes my face light up.”</p><p>Rodriguez credits the team’s recent success on the magic wand they've been waving from the dugout, not the pontiff. But the team really found what it needed in the recent trade for pitcher Luis Castillo, he said.</p><p>“I grew up in the World Series run, and that was magic to me,” Rodriguez said. “This team seems like they could make a magical run.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Jeff Agrest</i></p>

entries.title: 2 tornadoes packing winds of 86 to 110 mph hit Chicago area, toppling trees and leaving 250,000 without power
entries.summary: <p>Two tornadoes hit the Chicago area on Tuesday in a fast-moving storm with 99 mph winds that left a path of destruction in the south suburbs and cut power to hundreds of thousands.</p><p>The National Weather Service said two tornadoes with gusts of 86 to 110 mph hit southern Cook County, on its border with Will County, and in eastern Will County.</p><p>Survey teams continued working to confirm possible tornadoes near Homer Glen, Tinley Park, Crete and Manhattan — just weeks after surveyors confirmed <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/seven-7-confirmed-tornadoes-weather-service-illinois-monday-storms" target="_blank" >seven tornadoes hit</a> the south and west suburbs in a different storm.</p><p>The storms also damaged parts of Chicago. around 2 inches of rain fell and a top wind gust of 99 mph was recorded in Gary, Indiana, around 11 a.m., according to the weather service.</p><p>There were reports of 81 mph winds in South Barrington, and 70 mph in Oak Lawn.</p><p>The strongest squalls erupted through a “kind of a corridor,’’ south and southwest throughout Cook County and adjacent collar counties, weather service meteorologist Scott Baker said.</p><p>Damage was reported across the Chicago region.</p><p>In south suburban Mokena, storms took down trees in several places, cutting power to many homes.</p><p>Rick Johnson, a Mokena resident of more than 30 years, said his home lost power — the same as it did last month for four days during another round of storms. He said he's never experienced so many powerful and destructive storms in a single summer.</p><p>"It's been an odd year," he said.</p><p>In south suburban Homewood, officials reported downed power lines, large trees and debris blocking roadways and intersections.</p><p>"Areas south of 183rd Street appear to have sustained substantial damage," village officials said on social media. More than two-thirds of the town lost power in the storm, they said.</p><p>In Orland Park, the storm tore off the roof of an animal daycare. Workers could be seen repairing the roof of Midwest Animal Hospital, at 11205 W. 183rd St., later in the afternoon.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" damage, including power outages, damage to rooftops, inoperable traffic lights, shattered windows, flooding, and downed trees, poles and power lines."</p><p>Power lines fell into the roadway on 175th Street in Tinley Park and on Kedzie Avenue in Flossmoor, according to Cook County emergency alerts.</p><p>People on social media posted photos of downed trees in Gary and Munster, Indiana, and several south and southwest suburbs.</p><p>Ald. Raymond Lopez (15th) posted photos of several downed trees in his ward that covers the Southwest Side.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Some examples of the unreported tree emergencies we found in the 15th Ward! <a href="https://t.co/7SWjEJlB0c">pic.twitter.com/7SWjEJlB0c</a></p>— Ald. The number of outages was down to 250,000 later Tuesday afternoon.</p><p>The storms also wreaked havoc on air travel.</p><p>Nearly 300 flights were canceled at O'Hare Airport, according to FlyChicago.com. At Midway Airport conditions were less severe, with only a handful of cancellations.</p><p>In northwest Indiana, Portage Township canceled the first day of classes on Wednesday due to the damage. Portage Mayor Austin Bonta wrote on social media that the damage from the storm was extensive. </p><p>"I just spoke with our Chief of Police.
